A .py file of reusable code you bring into another file with import
A built-in feature that only works inside Jupyter notebooks
A folder that cannot contain any Python files

questions.q: What's the practical difference between `import json` and `from json import loads`?
options: from json import loads is invalid Python syntax
import json only works with third-party packages, never the standard library
There is no difference — they behave identically in every case
The first requires prefixing with json. (like json.loads), while the second pulls loads directly into your namespace with no prefix
questions.explain: import json requires the json. prefix on every use; from json import loads lets you call loads() directly.

questions.q: Which of these modules is part of Python's standard library and needs no installation?
options: pandas
openai
json
requests
questions.explain: json ships with Python itself; openai, requests, and pandas are third-party packages installed separately with pip.

options: Automatically imports requests into every file in the project
Installs the third-party requests package so it can then be imported
Is only used for installing Python itself, not packages
Permanently modifies Python's own standard library
questions.explain: pip install downloads and installs a third-party package; you still need a separate import statement to use it in your code.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what mechanism does every AI provider's SDK use?
options: Downloading a .exe file instead of using pip
SDKs cannot be imported, only called from the command line
A completely separate installation system unlike any other Python package
pip install the package, then import it — the exact same pattern as any other third-party package
questions.explain: AI provider SDKs are ordinary third-party packages — pip install openai, then import openai, same as requests or pandas.
